newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Fraser optimistic on Australian productivity.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Fraser optimistic on Australian productivity.

text.p: Retiring Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) governor Bernie Fraser said there was reason to be optimistic about Australian productivity growth.
"Productivity growth is the key to sustained economic growth," he said in a speech to BZW's Australia Day seminar in Tokyo. A copy of his speech was released here.
"On this point we have grounds for optimism about Australia."
While Australian productivity growth had slowed after recovery from the early 1980s recession, it had continued at a strong pace into the 1990s.

"In the current cycle, productivity in the market sector of the economy has grown at an average of 2.75 percent a year, compared with two percent a year in the corresponding period of the 1980's cycle," Fraser said.
So there seemed to have been a structural lift in productivity growth in the 1990s, he said.
"Indeed, it would have been most disappointing if such a lift were not occurring, given the substantial microeconomic reforms which have been implemented over the past decade."
The new Liberal-National government, elected in March, plans to change the industrial relations system to promote individual work contracts for each workplace while reducing union power.

"To the extent that such proposals, when implemented, help to better align wage increases with productivity increases, they will improve the prospects for sustained growth and low inflation," Fraser said.
But businesses would continue to be pressured by the same reforms that had already delivered productivity gains, especially exposure to greater domestic and international competition, he said.
"Employers and employees who attempt to ignore these irreversible changes are likely to suffer heavy penalties in terms of squeezes on profits and jobs, and lost opportunities for both."
